input.title: Ask git once where the suite asked twice, and stop re-proving one seed 74 times
input.body:
Round two of the suite profiling, from the driver table in #2062. Three changes that need nobody's judgement call; the ones that do are in the conversation, not here.

**60.1s / 62.0s → 53.5s / 53.4s** on `main`'s own commit, 3669 tests green in both arms, both sweeps clean.

## 1. Every rehearsal fixture was re-proving one seed record

`apply-vendor-set` was the single most expensive command in the suite — 148 invocations, 43.4s of CPU, more than every `git commit` in the suite combined. It ran twice per rehearsal because the runner's second converge is conditional on a migration record having rewritten the declaration, and that condition was true **74 times out of 74**.

The record was one `declarePacks` seed — `claude-code-web-users-support`, which no fixture declared — so every fixture modelled a member from before it landed and paid a second full vendor-set application to re-prove the same seed. The fixtures now start where a real member already is, carrying the pack with the config its record writes. That is the reasoning the helper already applies to `core`, for the same reason: a fixture modelling a shape the fleet no longer has hides regressions rather than catching them. `core-undeclared` bypasses the helper, so the seed-then-reconverge path keeps its fixture.

**148 → 95 invocations, 74/74 → 20/74 rehearsals.** Read off each fixture's declaration before and after the applier, not inferred. The remaining 20 are fixtures a record genuinely heals — executor and workflow shapes carrying scheduler workflows without declaring the tasks pack, plus `dormant` — so the second pass now runs where it is exercised instead of everywhere.

## 2. Ask git once where the context asked twice

Two paired subprocesses in `buildContext` become one each, both documented at the site with the git behaviour that makes them equivalent.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `ls-files` + `ls-files --others --exclude-standard` | 2248 | **1124** (`ls-files -c -o --exclude-standard -t`) |
| `diff --name-only --diff-filter=d` / `=D` | 2254 | **1130** (`--name-status`, + 6 rename fallbacks) |
| `git init` for `base` fixtures | 286 | **105** (they copy the template and move `main`) |
| all subprocesses, whole suite | 15,647 | **13,273** (−15.2%) |

The rename case is why I declined the `--name-status` merge in #2062. It was fuzzed over 200 random histories — renames, deletions, additions, edits, unicode, spaced and nested paths — and `--name-status` with `D` dropped reproduces `--name-only --diff-filter=d` exactly, order included, because git orders a rename entry under its destination. The fallback to the original pair stays anyway for any diff carrying a rename or copy: nothing git *documents* promises two commands order a two-path entry alike, that order reaches `ctx.files`, and the measured price is 6 spawns in the entire suite.

Behaviour equivalence is proven, not assumed: a harness compares four combinations per case — old fixture/old context, old/new, new/old, new/new — over **26 shapes × both modes, all byte-identical in all four paths**, snapshotting every context field plus `readBase`, `addedLines`, `removedLines`, the derived vendored set, `commitsWithFiles()`, `introducedMergeCommits()` and `grepTracked()`. Shapes include renames whose destination reverses the sort order, rename+deletion+edit together, `.gitattributes` at three depths, `.gitignore`, unicode and spaced paths.

Two candidates from the same list were rejected with evidence rather than taken:
- **skipping `check-attr` when no `.gitattributes` is in scope** — attributes reach git from four places, only one of which is the tree; `core.attributesFile` and the system file resolve through git's whole config cascade, which this repo's own fixture helper writes into. A tree-only probe is not behaviour-preserving, and its failure mode is a wrong `ctx.files`.
- **dropping the fixture's second commit** — it is the sole producer of `ctx.commits` and `commitsWithFiles()`. That is an observable field change, and exactly the "a flagged case goes clean" hazard.

## 3. Call the check runners in-process where the case judges the module

`engine-tests/runner.test.mjs` went from **38 node-CLI spawns to 3**. A `runScriptInProcess` helper re-imports the entry point under a fresh query so its top-level body re-runs, swapping `argv` and the console channels and returning `spawnSync`'s `{status, stdout, stderr}` shape — so 24 of 26 cases kept their assertions verbatim.

It keeps spawning exactly where the *process* is the contract: the `--list` catalog test (the #2062 truncation surface, invisible to an in-process caller that sees every `console.log` land whole), one real-exit-status case, and the deleted-cwd reproduction. Each says so at the site.

The `process.exitCode` restore in that helper is load-bearing and proven so: deleting it makes the file exit 1 while every test reports pass.

## Verified, not just reported

This work came back from agents, so the load-bearing claims were re-run here: killing the findings printer turns **18 of 26** converted cases red; deleting the exitCode restore leaks a failing status; the `localSignalContext` call count was re-counted independently. The two branches were also never combined until this PR, so the A/B above is of the combination, not of either half.

PR is [#2074](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/2074). Three things left need your call — they're all changes to code that ships to members, which is the boundary you set.

questions.question: Building a check context runs ~9 git commands up front; most rules only ever read two of them. Making the rest compute on first read cuts the suite's git subprocesses by 64% (10,214 → 3,710) — but in production it saves ~35ms per CI sweep and nothing at all on the Stop hook, because work-scoped rules read every field. It also moves one thing: today building a context always refreshes the base branch ref; lazily, only a context someone reads does. One existing test depends on that.

options.label: Take it, refresh stays eager (Recommended)
options.description: Keep the base-ref refresh exactly where it is today, lazify everything after it. Gives up roughly a sixth of the saving, needs no test edit, and changes no contract.

options.label: Take it, fully lazy
options.description: Full saving. Accepts that 'every context refreshes the base ref' becomes 'every context that is used does', and edits the test that relies on the old guarantee.

options.label: Leave it alone
options.description: It buys ~35ms in production and nothing on the Stop hook; skip the engine churn and keep the suite as it is.

questions.question: The queue's signal collection re-reads the checkout on every call — four manifest probes, a workflows directory listing and a config read, all of which are pure functions of the repo root. That is 50,111 calls and ~300,000 failing syscalls in one test file, and a real scheduler tick over 20 tasks does ~40 redundant probe sets, with the executor repeating them at every pick. Fixing it measured ~3x on that file.

options.label: Take both, scoped to the collector (Recommended)
options.description: Cache the probe result for the life of one collector and hoist two per-call dynamic imports. Measured ~2.5x. The cache dies with the collector, so a code_work step rewriting the tree between two picks cannot be served stale data.

options.label: Take the import hoist only
options.description: Hoist the two per-call imports and leave the disk probes alone. Smaller, and touches nothing that reads the working tree.

options.label: Cache for the whole process
options.description: Fastest, but a long-running executor that rewrites the tree mid-run would then read its own stale answer.

options.label: Leave it alone
options.description: Keep the current behaviour and accept the cost in both the tests and real runs.

questions.question: The dispatch resolver prints and exits from eleven places inside itself, so each of its 29 tests has to pay for a whole process. Splitting it so the logic returns its result and a thin wrapper does the printing and exiting would let ~27 of those run in-process while 2–3 keep spawning to hold the exit-code contract your earlier decision recorded for that file.

options.label: Do the split (Recommended)
options.description: Worth ~1.8s. The returned code preserves the exit-code assertions; the wrapper keeps the CLI behaving identically.

options.label: Leave it alone
options.description: It is the smallest of the three and touches a file whose CLI shape you settled deliberately.

content.text: All three approved. Launching the implementations — the lazy-context one has to branch off my PR branch, since it edits the same file I just changed.

input.prompt:
Implement an APPROVED optimisation. Read CLAUDE.md and follow the repo's rules (it will be loaded for you).

**Base your work on the branch `claude/relaxed-meitner-pqhaq8`, NOT on `main`** — it already rewrote the two functions you are about to touch (`listFiles`, `diffLists` in `engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs`). In your worktree: `git switch -c perf/lazy-ctx claude/relaxed-meitner-pqhaq8`. Commit there; do not push, do not open a PR.

THE CHANGE: make `buildContext()` in `engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs` compute its work-scoping fields on first read instead of eagerly. A prior analysis prototyped this and measured it; you are implementing the approved variant, not re-deciding it.

Shape: a local `once()` memo per derived value, exposed as getters on the returned object.
```js
const once = (fn) => { let v, done = false; return () => (done ? v : (done = true, v = fn())); };
```
Lazify: `mergeBase`, `vsBase`, `scanned`, `allFiles`, `files`, `changedFiles`, `deleted`, `commits`, `branch`. Keep EAGER: `tracked`, `untracked`, `root`, `mode`, `config` (every rule reads them). Every method body that closed over the old values — `readBase`, `addedLines`, `removedLines`, `commitsWithFiles`, `introducedMergeCommits`, `onBaseBranch` — becomes a call (`mergeBase()`, `diffBase()`, `baseRef()`).

TWO CONDITIONS THE OWNER ATTACHED. Both are requirements, not suggestions:

1. **`baseRef` and `refreshBaseRef` STAY EAGER.** The owner chose this explicitly over full laziness. Today, building a context always refreshes the base ref; the fully-lazy version turns that into "only a context someone reads does", and `engine-tests/context.test.mjs:359` depends on the current guarantee — it calls `buildContext({root, mode:'changed'})`, **discards the result**, and asserts the refresh marker exists. Keeping `resolveBaseRef` + `refreshBaseRef` eager means that test needs no edit and no contract moves. It costs back the `cat-file --batch-check` saving (~1124 spawns in the suite); that is the accepted price. **Do not edit `context.test.mjs` to make a lazier version pass** — if you find yourself wanting to, you have drifted from the approved variant.

2. **Give every lazy property a setter** that overwrites it with a plain value. ESM is strict, so a getter-only property makes `ctx.files = …` throw. This repo has no such assignment, but the engine is vendored into member repos whose own local-pack rules we cannot see; a setter makes the change backward-compatible for them instead of a crash. Say so in a comment at the site.

HARD REQUIREMENTS:
1. `repo-context.mjs` is ENGINE code vendored to every member — a regression breaks the fleet.
2. PROVE EQUIVALENCE, don't assume it. There is an equivalence harness from the previous round at `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Claudinite/f3d8d7fb-9e09-5900-8222-0efd575b14b1/scratchpad/perf/equiv2.mjs` (and `equiv.mjs`) that snapshots the WHOLE context — every field, file contents, `readBase`, `addedLines`, `removedLines`, the derived vendored set, `commitsWithFiles()`, `introducedMergeCommits()`, `grepTracked()` — and compares old against new across ~26 repo shapes in both modes. Reuse and extend it; a getter must produce byte-identical output to the eager field. Note the harness compares a snapshot of `Object.keys`-style enumeration too — check that getters do not change what enumerates.
3. Check the things laziness specifically breaks, and report what you found: anything that spreads (`{...ctx}`), `JSON.stringify(ctx)`, `Object.keys(ctx)`, `for…in`, or assigns to a context field; the `work.mjs` wrapper (~line 71-80) that re-exposes fields; `work.mjs`'s `typeof this.ctx.removedLines !== 'function'` feature detection; and any caller that depends on a git error surfacing at build time rather than at first read.
4. Run the WHOLE suite green from the worktree root: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — expect 3669 tests. Also `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` and `node engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs`, both exit 0 (the world sweep prints ~189 advisories, 0 blocking — that is clean).
